title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about articulating criticality: turning critical reading into critical writing. By the end you will be able to synthesise several sources into an argument of your own, form a reasoned judgement and justify it, and articulate that judgement in the language of criticality and your discipline's own vocabulary.

These are the moves that mark advanced academic work. At this level 'be more critical' is no longer a note in the margin. The expectation is that you produce criticality on the page, building arguments, reaching judgements and defending them in writing a reader in your field will recognise.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: synthesise several interpretations or sources into a critical argument of your own
form a reasoned critical judgement and justify it with evidence
articulate critical judgement using the language of criticality and your discipline's own vocabulary.

title: In real academic practice
body: Articulating criticality is what advanced academic work rewards. Every essay that asks you to construct an argument, every dissertation that weighs competing evidence, every piece of writing judged on the quality of its reasoning draws on these moves. The same capability, to synthesise, judge and justify in writing, is what research and professional practice ask of you beyond your degree.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, synthesising sources into an argument of your own. Second, forming and justifying judgements. Third, articulating criticality in the language and vocabulary of your discipline. Each lesson builds on the one before, moving from argument to judgement to the words that carry them.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You already read critically: you engage with sources, analyse interpretations and weigh them. This lesson is about what you do with several of them at once. Synthesis is where critical reading becomes critical writing, because it asks you to build an argument of your own from more than one voice.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the aim is not to recognise synthesis but to produce it. You are expected to lead: to take a set of sources that do not agree and construct a defensible line through them that is recognisably your own.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what synthesis adds beyond summarising sources one at a time
recognise synthesis in a worked example that forms an argument from several sources
construct the line of an argument that draws several sources in {{context}} together.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Synthesis is the ability to draw together different interpretations or evidence in the formation and expression of your own argument. It is not the same as summary. A summary reports each source in turn. A synthesis sets them in relation to one another and uses that relation to build a position none of them stated alone.

This is the move that turns a reading list into an argument. When you synthesise, the sources stop being things you report and become evidence you marshal. The argument is yours, and the sources are there to do work for it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent piece of writing where you used several sources. Did you summarise them one by one, or build an argument that set them in relation? What is one place you could have synthesised rather than listed?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Synthesis draws several interpretations together into an argument of your own, rather than summarising each in turn. You can now explain what synthesis adds, recognise it in a worked example, and construct the line of an argument that sets sources in relation to one another. The next lesson turns that argument into a reasoned judgement you can justify.

title: Orientation
body: Synthesis gives you an argument built from several sources. A judgement is what that argument is for: a reasoned verdict on which interpretation, explanation or piece of evidence carries more weight. This lesson is about forming judgements that are defensible, and justifying them so a reader can see why.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to commit. Leaving the weighing to the reader is not enough. The work is to reach a position, state it in a form that can be challenged, and defend it with the evidence it rests on.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what turns a description into a judgement
recognise a well-formed judgement in a worked example
form a judgement of relative value about {{context}} and state the reasons it rests on.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A judgement is a reasoned verdict of relative value. It takes a characteristic two-part form: X is more important, or more secure, or more convincing than Y, because of the evidence or reasoning that supports it. The second part is what separates a judgement from an opinion. An opinion asserts; a judgement weighs and gives its grounds.

Forming a judgement means evaluating the alternatives before you decide, not choosing one and defending it afterwards. A judgement reached that way is defensible, because the reasons were there from the start and it survives the question 'why?'.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Recall a time you had to choose between two explanations or sources. Did you reach a judgement and say why, or describe both and leave it there? What reason could you have made explicit?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A judgement is a reasoned verdict of relative value, stated in a two-part form with the reasons it rests on. You can now tell a judgement from a description, recognise a well-formed one, and reach a judgement by weighing the alternatives and making your grounds explicit. The last lesson gives you the language to articulate it precisely.

title: Orientation
body: You can synthesise sources and reach a judgement. This lesson is about articulating that judgement so a reader can follow it. Criticality has a language of its own: connectives that signal how claims relate, and disciplinary terms that carry judgements in a single word. Using them well is itself a critical act.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level, precision in wording is part of the argument, not decoration. The expectation is that your language does the critical work visibly, so the reader can see each move you make from the words you choose.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use the connective language of criticality to signal critical moves in your writing
explain why discipline-specific vocabulary carries critical meaning in {{context}}
choose the wording that articulates a critical judgement precisely.

title: Concept: definition
body:
The language of criticality is the set of words that signal critical moves. Connectives such as 'however', 'therefore' and 'nevertheless' show the reader how your claims relate: where one view gives way to another, where a conclusion follows from evidence, where a point is conceded. Hedges such as 'arguably' or 'provisional' mark how far a claim can be pressed.

Discipline-specific vocabulary goes further. Within a field, certain words carry a precise, loaded meaning, so choosing the right term states a judgement the everyday word would leave unsaid. Articulating criticality means using this language deliberately, so the reasoning is visible in the writing.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at a recent judgement you wrote. Did its wording make the reasoning visible, or did a vague phrase hide the move? Which word could you have chosen to say exactly what you meant?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Articulating criticality means using the language of criticality deliberately: connectives that signal how claims relate, hedges that mark how far a claim can be pressed, and disciplinary terms that carry judgements precisely. You can now signal critical moves in your writing, explain why discipline-specific vocabulary matters, and choose wording that articulates a judgement exactly. With synthesis, judgement and language in place, you can be critical on the page.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Articulating criticality is now something you can do on the page. You can synthesise several sources into an argument of your own, rather than summarising each in turn. You can form a reasoned judgement of relative value and justify it with the evidence it rests on. And you can articulate that judgement in the language of criticality and your discipline's own vocabulary, so the reasoning is visible in the writing. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, articulating criticality is something you practise in every piece of advanced work. Each argument you construct from several sources, each judgement you reach and defend, each term you choose for its precise meaning is this capability at work. It is also what research and professional life reward: the ability to weigh evidence and argue a position, in writing, with reasons.

title: Explore the concept
body: Synthesis is a process that turns several sources into an argument of your own. Move through the four stages to see how.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal it. Work through all four in order.

_items.title: Gather the interpretations
_items.body: You collect the positions several sources take on your question, in their own terms, not yet judging them. Synthesis starts with more than one voice on the table.

_items.title: Map where they meet and part
_items.body: You set the interpretations against each other. Where do they agree, where do they conflict, and what does each rest on? The pattern between them is the raw material of your argument.

_items.title: Form your own line
_items.body: From that map you build a position none of the sources stated alone: your reading of what the weight of the evidence supports. This is the step that turns reading into authorship.

_items.title: Express it as an argument
_items.body: You write the position so a reader can follow it, drawing each source in where it does work for your line rather than summarising them one after another.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four things that make a verdict a judgement rather than an opinion or a description. Read each card.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Information cards about what makes a critical judgement.

_items.title: More than a description
_items.subtitle: The core move
_items.text: A description reports what the sources say. A judgement states what you make of them: which interpretation carries more weight, and on what grounds.

_items.title: A two-part form
_items.subtitle: Its shape
_items.text: A judgement has a claim of relative value and the reasons behind it: X is more secure than Y, because of the evidence that supports it.

_items.title: Weighed, not assumed
_items.subtitle: What earns it
_items.text: A judgement is reached by evaluating the alternatives, not by preferring one from the start. The weighing is what makes it defensible.

_items.title: Open to challenge
_items.subtitle: Its honesty
_items.text: A strong judgement names what would count against it and claims no more certainty than the evidence will bear.

_term.definition: Marks what follows as a conclusion drawn from the evidence just given, not a fresh assertion.

_passage.text: to draw a conclusion from evidence, and

_term.definition: Presents a claim as open to debate. Used well, it claims no more certainty than the evidence supports.

_passage.text: to mark a claim as contestable rather than settled. Within a field,

_term.definition: Words that carry a precise, loaded meaning within a field's discourse, so that the right term states a judgement the everyday word would leave unsaid.

_passage.text: terms carry judgements of their own, so choosing the right word is itself a critical act.
The same holds for stance. A writer reaches for

_term.definition: Grants the previous point yet holds the argument's line, showing you have weighed the objection rather than avoided it.

_passage.text: to concede a point without surrendering the argument, and for

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students writing about the same debate, using three sources that partly disagree.

{{learner-a}} takes each source in turn: the first argues one thing, the second another, the third adds a further point. Each paragraph is accurate, and the sources are all there. But {{learner-a}} has set them side by side, leaving the reader to work out what it all amounts to. No position of {{learner-a}}'s own emerges. This is summary, not synthesis.

{{learner-b}} sets the three sources against each other. Where do they agree, where do they pull apart, and what does each claim rest on? From that mapping {{learner-b}} builds a line of argument none of the sources stated alone, drawing each source in where it does work for that line. This is synthesis: the sources serve an argument the writer owns.

Both students read the same three sources. Only {{learner-b}} turned them into an argument rather than a list.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students are asked which of two competing studies better supports a claim.

{{learner-a}} writes that the first study found a large effect and the second a smaller one, and that both were carefully conducted. This is accurate, and it is a description: it reports what each study says but stops short of saying which carries more weight. The reader is left to judge.

{{learner-b}} writes that the first study's claim is the more secure, because its sample was larger and its design controlled for the rival explanation the second study left open. This is a judgement: it states relative value and gives the reasons it rests on, in the two-part form a defensible judgement takes.

Both students understood the studies. Only {{learner-b}} reached a judgement, rather than leaving the weighing to the reader.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students write up the same judgement about a disputed finding.

{{learner-a}} writes: this idea is good, and the other one is not as good, so the first is better. The judgement is there in outline, but the language is flat. Nothing signals how the claims relate, and no term carries the precise meaning the field would expect. The reader cannot see the reasoning move.

{{learner-b}} writes: the first account is the more robust; however, it rests on a contested measure, so its advantage is provisional rather than settled. The connectives mark the critical moves, and the disciplinary terms carry judgements of their own. The same position is now articulated with precision.

Both students reached a similar view. Only {{learner-b}} articulated it in the language of criticality.

title: Synthesis moves
body: These moves turn the idea into something you do. Try them on your next piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I gathered what each source actually claims, in its own terms?
Have I mapped where the sources agree and where they conflict?
Have I identified what each claim rests on?
Have I formed a position of my own that none of the sources stated alone?
Have I drawn each source in where it does work for my argument, rather than summarising it?
Could a reader see my line of argument, not just a list of sources?

title: Forming a judgement
body: These moves turn the idea into something you do. Try them on your next piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I said which option carries more weight, not just described them both?
Have I given the reasons my judgement rests on?
Did I weigh the alternatives before deciding, rather than starting from a preference?
Have I stated the judgement in its two-part form: X over Y, because?
Have I named what would count against my judgement?
Have I claimed no more certainty than the evidence supports?

title: Articulating the judgement
body: These moves turn the idea into something you do. Try them on your next piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I used connectives to signal each critical move to the reader?
Have I used 'however' or 'yet' where my argument turns to a counter-view?
Have I used 'therefore' or 'so' only where a conclusion follows from evidence?
Have I hedged contestable claims rather than overstating them?
Have I chosen disciplinary terms for their precise meaning, not their sound?
Would a reader in my field recognise the judgement in my wording?

title: Formative check: what synthesis adds
displayTitle: Which of these best describes synthesis, rather than summary?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option best describes synthesis rather than summary?

_items.text: Drawing several sources together into an argument of your own that none stated alone.
_items.feedback: Yes. Synthesis builds a position from the relation between sources.

_items.text: Reporting each source's main point in turn.
_items.feedback: That is summary; it reports sources rather than relating them.

_items.text: Choosing the single strongest source and following it.
_items.feedback: Following one source is not synthesis; synthesis works across several.

_items.text: Listing the sources that agree with your view.
_items.feedback: A list of agreeing sources is not an argument built from their relation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Synthesis draws sources together into an argument of your own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that builds a position from the relation between sources.
_incorrect.final: Synthesis draws several sources into an argument none stated alone. Reporting in turn, following one source, or listing agreement are not synthesis.

title: Formative check: recognising synthesis
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second writer's paragraph a synthesis rather than a summary?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second writer's paragraph a synthesis?

_items.text: It built a position of its own by setting the sources against each other.
_items.feedback: Yes. Relating the sources to build a position is synthesis.

_items.text: It described each source accurately, one after another.
_items.feedback: Describing each in turn is summary, not synthesis.

_items.text: It quoted the most authoritative source at length.
_items.feedback: A long quotation does not build an argument from several sources.

_items.text: It chose the source that best fit the essay's point.
_items.feedback: Picking one fitting source is not synthesising several.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second writer set the sources in relation and built a position of their own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the writer DID across the sources, beyond reporting them.
_incorrect.final: The paragraph was a synthesis because it set the sources against each other and built a position of its own. Describing, quoting or picking one source are not synthesis.

title: Formative check: constructing a synthesis
displayTitle: You are building an argument from three sources in {{context}} that partly disagree. Which move produces a synthesis?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move produces a synthesis from three disagreeing sources?

_items.text: Set the three against each other and state the position their balance supports.
_items.feedback: Yes. That builds a synthesis from the relation between the sources in {{context}}.

_items.text: Summarise each in a separate paragraph and stop there.
_items.feedback: Separate summaries leave the reader to do the synthesising.

_items.text: Follow whichever source is the most recent.
_items.feedback: Recency is not a reason to follow one source over the others.

_items.text: Report only the points on which all three agree.
_items.feedback: Reporting only agreement drops the tension that an argument works with.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, setting the sources in relation and stating the position their balance supports is synthesis.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that relates the sources rather than reporting them separately.
_incorrect.final: A synthesis in {{context}} sets the sources against each other and states the position their balance supports. Separate summaries, following the newest, or reporting only agreement are not synthesis.

title: Formative check: judgement versus description
displayTitle: Which of these sentences is a judgement rather than a description?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which sentence is a judgement rather than a description?

_items.text: The first study's claim is the more secure, because its sample was larger and better controlled.
_items.feedback: Yes. It states relative value and gives the reason, so it is a judgement.

_items.text: The first study reports a large effect and the second a small one.
_items.feedback: That reports what the studies found; it is a description.

_items.text: Both studies were published in peer-reviewed journals.
_items.feedback: That is a fact about the studies, not a verdict on their value.

_items.text: The two studies used different methods.
_items.feedback: Noting a difference is description; it reaches no verdict.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Stating relative value with a reason is a judgement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the sentence that says which carries more weight, and why.
_incorrect.final: A judgement states relative value and gives its reason. The other sentences report findings, facts or differences without reaching a verdict.

title: Formative check: a well-formed judgement
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second writer's verdict a well-formed judgement?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second writer's verdict a well-formed judgement?

_items.text: It claimed relative value and gave the reasons it rested on.
_items.feedback: Yes. The two-part form, claim plus reasons, is what makes it well formed.

_items.text: It stated a firm opinion without qualification.
_items.feedback: A firm opinion without grounds is assertion, not a judgement.

_items.text: It summarised both studies even-handedly.
_items.feedback: Even-handed summary describes; it reaches no verdict.

_items.text: It preferred the study the writer already favoured.
_items.feedback: Starting from a preference is the opposite of weighing the alternatives.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The verdict claimed relative value and gave its reasons.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the two-part form: a claim of value, and the reasons behind it.
_incorrect.final: The verdict was well formed because it claimed relative value and gave its reasons. An unqualified opinion, an even-handed summary, or a prior preference are not judgements.

title: Formative check: forming a judgement
displayTitle: You must judge two competing explanations in {{context}}. Which response is a justified judgement?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response is a justified judgement of two competing explanations?

_items.text: State which explanation the evidence supports more, and say why.
_items.feedback: Yes. A claim of relative value with its reasons is a justified judgement in {{context}}.

_items.text: Describe both explanations and leave the choice open.
_items.feedback: Leaving the choice open reaches no judgement.

_items.text: Choose the explanation your tutor prefers.
_items.feedback: Deferring to a preference is not weighing the evidence.

_items.text: Pick the explanation that is easier to summarise.
_items.feedback: Ease of summary is not a ground for judging relative value.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, stating which the evidence supports more, and why, is a justified judgement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the response that reaches a verdict and gives its grounds.
_incorrect.final: A justified judgement in {{context}} states which explanation the evidence supports more, and why. Describing both, deferring to a preference, or choosing the simplest are not judgements.

title: Formative check: signalling a critical move
displayTitle: You want to signal that the next claim runs against the one before it. Which word does that work?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which word signals that the next claim runs against the one before?

_items.text: However.
_items.feedback: Yes. 'However' marks a turn to a competing view.

_items.text: Therefore.
_items.feedback: 'Therefore' marks a conclusion that follows, not a contrast.

_items.text: Furthermore.
_items.feedback: 'Furthermore' adds a point in the same direction, not against it.

_items.text: For example.
_items.feedback: 'For example' introduces an illustration, not a counter-claim.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'However' signals a turn to a competing view.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which connective marks a contrast rather than an addition or a conclusion?
_incorrect.final: 'However' signals a contrast. 'Therefore' concludes, 'furthermore' adds, and 'for example' illustrates.

title: Formative check: why precise vocabulary matters
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the precise disciplinary term do more critical work than the everyday word?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the precise disciplinary term do more critical work than the everyday word?

_items.text: It carried a defined meaning in the field, so it made a judgement the vague word left unsaid.
_items.feedback: Yes. A loaded disciplinary term states a judgement the everyday word cannot.

_items.text: It made the writing sound more formal.
_items.feedback: Sounding formal is not the same as doing critical work.

_items.text: It was longer and more technical.
_items.feedback: Length and technicality alone do not carry judgement.

_items.text: It avoided repeating an earlier word.
_items.feedback: Avoiding repetition is a style point, not a critical one.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The disciplinary term carried a defined meaning that stated a judgement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about meaning the field attaches to the term.
_incorrect.final: The term did critical work because it carried a defined meaning in the field, stating a judgement the vague word left unsaid. Formality, length or variety are not the point.

title: Formative check: articulating precisely
displayTitle: Writing up a judgement in {{context}}, which wording articulates it most precisely?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which wording articulates a judgement most precisely?

_items.text: This evidence is stronger because it rests on a larger, better-controlled sample.
_items.feedback: Yes. It states the judgement and the ground precisely, as {{context}} expects.

_items.text: This evidence is obviously the best.
_items.feedback: 'Obviously the best' asserts without a ground.

_items.text: This evidence seems quite good, really.
_items.feedback: A vague phrase hides the judgement rather than articulating it.

_items.text: This evidence is nice and clear.
_items.feedback: 'Nice and clear' says nothing about relative value or grounds.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, naming the judgement and its ground is the precise articulation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the wording that states both the verdict and the reason.
_incorrect.final: The precise wording states the judgement and its ground. 'Obviously the best', 'quite good really' and 'nice and clear' assert or hedge without reasons.

body: What distinguishes a synthesis from a summary of the same sources?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What distinguishes a synthesis from a summary?

_items.text: It builds a position of your own by setting the sources in relation to one another.
_items.feedback: Yes. Synthesis builds a position from the relation between sources.

_items.text: It reports each source more accurately.
_items.feedback: Accuracy of reporting is not what makes a synthesis.

_items.text: It uses more sources than a summary.
_items.feedback: Number of sources does not distinguish synthesis from summary.

_items.text: It quotes the sources at greater length.
_items.feedback: Longer quotation is not synthesis.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Synthesis builds a position from the relation between the sources.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what synthesis does with the sources.

body: You have three sources that disagree. Which approach produces a synthesis?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach produces a synthesis from three disagreeing sources?

_items.text: Set them against each other and argue the position their balance supports.
_items.feedback: Yes. That relates the sources into an argument of your own.

_items.text: Summarise each in its own paragraph.
_items.feedback: Separate summaries are not a synthesis.

_items.text: Follow the most recent source.
_items.feedback: Recency is not a ground for following one source.

_items.text: Report only what all three share.
_items.feedback: Reporting only agreement drops the tension an argument works with.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Setting the sources in relation and arguing the balance is synthesis.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the approach that relates the sources.

body: Which of these is a judgement rather than a description?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these is a judgement rather than a description?

_items.text: The first explanation is the more convincing, because it accounts for evidence the second cannot.
_items.feedback: Yes. It states relative value and gives the reason.

_items.text: The two explanations differ in several ways.
_items.feedback: Noting differences is description.

_items.text: Both explanations appear in the set reading.
_items.feedback: That is a fact, not a verdict.

_items.text: The first explanation is longer than the second.
_items.feedback: Length is not a judgement of value.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A judgement states relative value with a reason.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option reaches a verdict and says why?

body: What makes a critical judgement defensible?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What makes a critical judgement defensible?

_items.text: It weighs the alternatives and makes the reasons it rests on explicit.
_items.feedback: Yes. Weighing and explicit reasons make it defensible.

_items.text: It is stated with great confidence.
_items.feedback: Confidence is not a ground; it can overstate the evidence.

_items.text: It agrees with the most cited source.
_items.feedback: Agreement with a popular source is not a justification.

_items.text: It avoids committing to either side.
_items.feedback: Avoiding commitment reaches no judgement at all.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing the alternatives and giving explicit reasons makes a judgement defensible.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what lets a judgement survive the question 'why?'.

body: You want to signal that a conclusion follows from the evidence you have given. Which word does that?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which word signals that a conclusion follows from the evidence?

_items.text: Therefore.
_items.feedback: Yes. 'Therefore' marks a conclusion drawn from evidence.

_items.text: However.
_items.feedback: 'However' marks a contrast, not a conclusion.

_items.text: For example.
_items.feedback: 'For example' introduces an illustration.

_items.text: Meanwhile.
_items.feedback: 'Meanwhile' marks time, not inference.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'Therefore' signals a conclusion drawn from the evidence.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which connective marks inference rather than contrast or illustration?

body: Why does a precise disciplinary term often do more critical work than an everyday word?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does a precise disciplinary term do more critical work?

_items.text: It carries a defined meaning in the field, stating a judgement the vague word leaves unsaid.
_items.feedback: Yes. A loaded disciplinary term states a judgement the everyday word cannot.

_items.text: It makes the writing sound more academic.
_items.feedback: Sounding academic is not critical work.

_items.text: It is longer and more technical.
_items.feedback: Length and technicality alone carry no judgement.

_items.text: It avoids repetition.
_items.feedback: Avoiding repetition is a style point, not a critical one.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A disciplinary term carries a defined meaning that states a judgement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the meaning the field attaches to the term.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: synthesising sources into an argument of your own, forming and justifying a judgement, and articulating it in the language of criticality. On their own they are three separate moves. This lesson brings them together into one practice of critical writing you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not asked to learn the three moves again. The aim is to see them as one connected practice rather than three separate ideas, so critical writing carries on through the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together synthesis, reasoned judgement and the language of criticality as one practice of critical writing
recognise critical writing at work in an example that uses all three moves together
plan how you will write critically in your {{context}} work beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Critical writing is the three moves working as one. You synthesise several sources into an argument of your own, you form a reasoned judgement about what that argument supports, and you articulate it in precise critical language. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the parts of that single act.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, critical writing is one connected act, not three exercises done in turn. As you build an argument from your sources, you are already weighing them towards a judgement, and the words you choose carry that judgement to the reader. A short piece written this way is worth more than three moves practised apart.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of writing you have coming up. How will you draw your sources into an argument, reach a judgement, and word it so a reader can follow each move?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Critical writing is strongest when the three moves work as one. You synthesise your sources into an argument, form a reasoned judgement, and articulate it in precise language, all in the same piece. It is the three together, not any one alone, that makes writing critical.

See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The steps as one process
body: Critical writing builds up as a sequence of moves. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Gather
_items.body: Gather the sources and set them against each other to see where they agree and conflict.

_items.title: Synthesise
_items.body: Draw them together into a line of argument that is your own.

_items.title: Judge
_items.body: Form a reasoned judgement about what the argument supports, and state the reasons for it.

_items.title: Articulate
_items.body: Articulate the judgement in precise critical language so a reader can follow each move.

_diagram.title: Building a piece of critical writing

title: Worked example
body: Two students answer the same question using the same sources. One builds the argument, reaches a judgement, then struggles to word it, so the reasoning stays hidden. The other works the three moves together from the start, and the argument, judgement and wording hold as one clear piece.

title: Working with the cycle
body: Use these to keep the three moves working together, rather than treating them as separate tasks.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I drawn my sources into an argument of my own, rather than summarising them one by one?
Does my argument reach a judgement, not just describe the sources?
Have I given the reasons my judgement rests on?
Does my wording signal each critical move, so a reader can follow it?
Have I used the three moves together in one piece, rather than as separate exercises?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat synthesis, judgement and critical language as one practice rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it better to treat synthesis, judgement and critical language as one practice rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it better to treat synthesis, judgement and critical language as one practice rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because they do their work together: an argument carries a judgement, and critical language makes that judgement visible to a reader.
_items.feedback: Yes. In real writing the three moves support one another in the same piece.

_items.text: Because doing all three at once takes less thought than doing them one at a time.
_items.feedback: The point is not less effort. It is that the moves work together.

_items.text: Because only one of the three moves actually matters in a finished piece of writing.
_items.feedback: All three matter. The point is that they work as one.

_items.text: Because treating them separately means you never have to reach a judgement.
_items.feedback: A judgement is part of critical writing, not something to avoid.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three moves do their work together in one piece of critical writing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how an argument, a judgement and precise language support each other in the same piece.

displayTitle: A student writes an essay that draws three sources into an argument, reaches a judgement about which view is stronger, and words it so each step is clear. What does this show?
body: A student writes an essay that draws three sources into an argument, reaches a judgement about which view is stronger, and words it so each step is clear. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student writes an essay that draws three sources into an argument, reaches a judgement about which view is stronger, and words it so each step is clear. What does this show?

_items.text: That critical writing works as one practice: the argument, the judgement and the wording all do their work in the same piece.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three moves ran together in one connected act of writing.

_items.text: That the student used too many sources for one essay.
_items.feedback: The number of sources is not the point. The three moves worked together.

_items.text: That only strong students can write this way.
_items.feedback: This is something you can practise, whatever your starting point.

_items.text: That precise wording is the only move that matters.
_items.feedback: Wording carries the judgement, but the argument and judgement matter too.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Synthesis, judgement and critical language worked together in one piece.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the argument, the judgement and the wording worked together.

displayTitle: You want to write more critically in your {{context}} work this term. Which plan best treats the three moves as one practice?
body: You want to write more critically in your {{context}} work this term. Which plan best treats the three moves as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to write more critically in your your subject work this term. Which plan best treats the three moves as one practice?

_items.text: In each piece, draw your sources into an argument, reach a judgement, and word it precisely, so the three moves work together.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three moves support one another in the same piece of writing.

_items.text: Practise synthesis this month, judgement next month, and critical language the month after, keeping them apart.
_items.feedback: Keeping them apart misses the point. They work together in one piece.

_items.text: Focus only on precise wording and leave the argument and judgement to look after themselves.
_items.feedback: Wording cannot carry a piece on its own. All three moves are needed.

_items.text: Write the argument first, then add a judgement only if a marker asks for one.
_items.feedback: A judgement is part of critical writing, not an optional extra.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Using the three moves together, in each piece, is critical writing as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The strongest plan uses synthesis, judgement and critical language together in the same piece.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What does it mean to treat synthesis, judgement and critical language as one practice?
body: What does it mean to treat synthesis, judgement and critical language as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to treat synthesis, judgement and critical language as one practice?

_items.text: You use all three together in the same piece, so they support one another.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three moves work together in one piece.

_items.text: You do each one in a separate piece of writing.
_items.feedback: The moves work together, not apart.

_items.text: You choose the one move that suits you and ignore the rest.
_items.feedback: All three moves are needed.

_items.text: You keep the three moves apart so they do not interfere.
_items.feedback: They are meant to work together, not separately.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student drafts an essay, builds an argument from several sources, reaches a judgement, and words each move precisely. Which best describes what they have done?
body: A student drafts an essay, builds an argument from several sources, reaches a judgement, and words each move precisely. Which best describes what they have done?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student drafts an essay, builds an argument from several sources, reaches a judgement, and words each move precisely. Which best describes what they have done?

_items.text: They have written critically, using the three moves together as one practice.
_items.feedback: Yes. Synthesis, judgement and language worked as one.

_items.text: They have summarised the sources one by one.
_items.feedback: A summary reports each source in turn; this did more.

_items.text: They have described the sources without reaching a judgement.
_items.feedback: The student did reach a judgement.

_items.text: They have used critical language but formed no argument.
_items.feedback: An argument was built from several sources.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
